input.quote: If a third party claims or threatens a claim that Materials or Base Components IBM provides to Customer or uses in connection with the performance of the Services infringe that party's patent, trademark, copyright, or trade secret, then IBM will indemnify, defend and hold harmless the Customer, its Enterprise and their respective employees, officers, agents and directors against that claim or threatened claim at IBM's expense and pay all costs, damages, penalties and reasonable attorneys' fees that a court finally awards in connection with that claim
input.rationale: A Vendor IP indemnity is present and runs in our favour: § 8.1 has IBM defend, indemnify and hold harmless Customer and its Enterprise (including employees, officers, agents, directors) against third-party patent, trademark, copyright and trade secret claims relating to Materials or Base Components IBM provides or uses in performing the Services, with the standard procedure (prompt notice, IBM control, cooperation — and IBM reimbursing our cooperation costs) and the usual mitigation remedies (procure continued use, modify, replace, or credit up to twelve months of charges). Exclusions are the customary ones (Customer-supplied items, Customer modifications, combinations with non-IBM products, non-IBM hardware/software/data). This sits at the playbook fallback position, so we are not redlining it. Noted but not flagged: the indemnity does not extend to IBM's breach of law, data breach or gross negligence/wilful misconduct (preferred position), the refund remedy is capped at twelve months of charges, and our § 8.2 indemnity is broader than the preferred Customer-content-only scope (notably Services Recipient claims related to the Services), though § 8.2(c) relieves us to the extent IBM's bad faith, wilful misconduct, gross negligence or breach caused the damage. These are sub-elements short of preferred and can be raised as trade requests rather than as a critical deviation; the liability super-cap treatment for indemnities is addressed under the limitation-of-liability rule.
